rule_name: Bury Scale Inside a Fast List, Deliberately
quote: They stay two hours. They talk about a teacher's car, and about whether Ruth's brother is getting in, which he is, and they argue about the word *hither*
why: this inverts the rule's intended split: the ordinary, emotionally legible material (two hours of friend banter) is the thing compressed into a fast enumerated list, while the extraordinary material later (Sam against seven armed men) gets full scene-time, when the rule calls for the reverse
suggestion: give the diner conversation its own beat or two of real scene time (one exchange rendered, e.g. the *hither* argument played out in dialogue) and let a later ordinary passage, not the fight, absorb the list compression

rule_name: Sentence Rhythm, Break the Subject-Verb-Object Drumbeat
quote: He hits one in the side of the leg and the leg stops working. He hits the next twice in the body and that one sits down.
why: three consecutive sentences share an identical He-verb-object-and-result shape, producing exactly the flat reportorial drumbeat the rule warns against
suggestion: vary the openings and subordinate one clause: "One takes a hit to the leg and stops working it; the next, hit twice in the body, sits down where he stands."

rule_name: Sentence Rhythm, Break the Subject-Verb-Object Drumbeat
quote: He goes past the muzzle and takes the wrist and turns it out and down. The man bends.
why: a run of same-shape short declaratives (He-verb..., The man bends., Sam holds him there) with no varied opening or subordination, reading as a witness statement
suggestion: combine: "Past the muzzle, he takes the wrist and turns it out and down until the man bends," folding the short beat into the longer one instead of stacking identical shapes

rule_name: Sentence Rhythm, Break the Subject-Verb-Object Drumbeat
quote: Sam has the wrist before it's straight and the man goes down into the one behind him. Sam strips that one on the ground and throws the pieces in two directions.
why: both sentences open with "Sam" as subject followed by the same verb-object cadence, repeating the drumbeat the rule flags rather than varying the sentence opening
suggestion: open the second sentence differently: "On the ground, he strips that one too, throwing the pieces in two directions."

rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
why: Sam's own physical action (stopping) and the dialogue it leads directly into are the same character's single continuous beat, but are split into two separate paragraphs by the blank line after "Sam stops walking."
suggestion: merge: "Sam stops walking. 'That's not stupid,' he says."

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
why: this opens a run of three consecutive dialogue lines (61, 63, 65) with zero attribution at all, worse than the rule's own overcorrected example, leaving the reader unable to tell which of the three watchers is speaking
suggestion: attribute at least one line with a beat, e.g. "'He's slow on the transitions,' Nadia says, elbows on the ledge."

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
why: "the whole thing" is one of the rule's explicitly named crutch phrases, used here as filler rather than pointing to anything specific
suggestion: cut it: "...and won't for so long that it becomes the funniest part of breakfast."

rule_name: Section 8: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (narrator evaluation/ranking, superlatives in narration)
why: this is the narrator ranking the moment's comedic value rather than letting the detail (sixty replies, one laughing face, Sam's silence) stand on its own, and it is a narration superlative of the kind the table says to cut
suggestion: delete the ranking and end on the image: "Somebody in the year above has sent one laughing face and nothing else, and Sam won't discuss it, and won't for so long that people start bringing it up just to watch him not answer."

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
why: "for a while" is named directly in the rule as a universal duration marker used regardless of what kind of moment is being timed, and it isn't replaced here with a real duration or image
suggestion: give a real beat instead: "Sam doesn't answer. He looks at the sidewalk for three more steps."

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
why: this is a bare verdict validating Nadia's suggestion instead of describing what makes it not stupid, the same ranking-without-evidence pattern the rule bans even though the specific wording differs from the listed examples
suggestion: "That's not stupid," he says. "She's on her feet nine hours a day, that's real endurance." or cut the verdict and let his next line (already in the text) carry it alone

rule_name: Section 11: Structure (stated thesis vs. concrete facts)
quote: That's what's left after everything else didn't work.
why: this closes Chloe's answer with an abstract thesis statement about criminality rather than a concrete fact, which the Structure section says to avoid even in dialogue: concrete facts land harder than a stated thesis
suggestion: cut the sentence and end on the concrete image already given: "If you were good at anything you wouldn't be behind a hardware store at two in the morning taking phones off teenagers."

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
why: exact-duration precision applied to a background character's nap, unconnected to any point-of-view character's anxiety or control, shows the manuscript's counting tic being used as reflexive narrative default rather than characterization
suggestion: drop the exact figure: "Nadia falls asleep sitting up and wakes on her own, finishing her sentence."

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
why: a bare four-word fragment with no subordination is the same simple sentence shape six-year-old Chloe used in chapter one; after roughly a decade of narrative time the syntax has not grown to reflect it
suggestion: let the older Sam's frustration build a real clause: "So if guns and numbers don't count for anything, what am I actually supposed to be training for."

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
quote: Three of them had guns, Ruth.
why: a single unsubordinated clause with a vocative tag is the same construction level chapter one's six-year-old dialogue used; nothing in the sentence's architecture signals years of growth
suggestion: give it a subordinate clause that shows the older reasoning: "Three of them had guns, Ruth, which is usually the part that's supposed to matter."

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
why: a flat four-word declarative with no subordination or qualification reads as syntactically younger than the characters' established age this late in the book, where structure should have grown even if the content stays plain
suggestion: let the concession carry more clause weight: "She'd take me apart, and it wouldn't even be close."
